title: Strategy Pattern
tagline: Swap algorithms at runtime without changing the code that uses them — compose behaviour, don't inherit it.

sections.content:
Picture a `Checkout` class responsible for processing payments. Version one supports only Stripe. Then PayPal is added — a new `if` branch appears inside `Checkout.pay()`. Then crypto, then buy-now-pay-later. Six months later you have a sprawling `switch` statement with dozens of lines of unrelated payment logic tangled inside a class that should know nothing about the internals of any payment provider. Every time a new payment method is requested, you reopen `Checkout`, risk breaking the existing ones, and add tests that are impossible to isolate.

This is the problem the **Strategy** pattern was designed to solve. It is one of the original Gang of Four (GoF) behavioural patterns, described in *Design Patterns* (1994), and it remains one of the most practically useful patterns in everyday software development. The core idea is deceptively simple: **define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one in its own object, and make them interchangeable behind a common interface**.

The class that needs the behaviour — called the **Context** — holds a reference to a **Strategy** object and delegates the variable part of its work entirely to that object. The Context never cares which concrete strategy is active. Strategies are swappable at construction time or at runtime, testable in complete isolation, and addable without a single modification to the Context.

In this chapter you will study the pattern from four angles: (1) the canonical structure and its participants, (2) a before-and-after refactor in JavaScript showing exactly what changes, (3) the mechanics of runtime selection and dependency injection, (4) comparisons with related patterns like Template Method, Command, and State, and (5) real-world usage in Passport.js, webpack, sorting APIs, and validation libraries. By the end, recognising where and when to apply Strategy will be second nature.

sections.caption: The three participants: Context delegates to a Strategy interface; ConcreteStrategies implement that interface independently. Adding a new payment method means a new class only — Context never changes.

sections.title: A GPS App with Interchangeable Routing Engines
sections.content:
A navigation app has one goal — get you from A to B — but multiple **routing strategies**: fastest route, shortest distance, avoid tolls, scenic route, cycling path. The map screen (the Context) renders the turn-by-turn display. It does not implement road-network algorithms. Instead it calls `router.getRoute(start, end)` and renders whatever comes back.

When the user taps 'Avoid Tolls', the app does not rewrite the map screen. It swaps the routing strategy object. The map screen is oblivious. It calls the same method signature on the new strategy and renders the new route.

This is the Strategy pattern in everyday life. The Context (map screen) is stable and closed for modification. The variable part (routing algorithm) is encapsulated behind a uniform interface and is open for extension by adding new strategy classes.

JavaScript's own `Array.prototype.sort(compareFn)` is a textbook built-in example. The sorting engine (TimSort under the hood) is fixed. The **comparison strategy** is the function you inject — `(a, b) => a.age - b.age` for sorting by age, `(a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)` for alphabetical order. The array is the Context; your callback is the ConcreteStrategy. You cannot get more mainstream than that.

sections.title: The Three Participants in Detail
sections.content:
**1. Strategy (the interface or duck-typed contract)**

In statically typed languages (Java, TypeScript) this is a formal interface: `interface PaymentStrategy { execute(data: PaymentData): PaymentResult; }`. In JavaScript it is an implicit contract — any object that has an `execute(data)` method qualifies. This duck-typing flexibility means strategies can be plain objects, arrow functions, or class instances, whichever suits the situation.

The strategy interface should be **narrow**. One method is ideal. If your strategy interface has five methods, that is a smell that you are trying to encapsulate too broad a concept — consider splitting into smaller strategies or using a different pattern.

**2. ConcreteStrategy (the algorithm)**

Each concrete strategy encapsulates one variant of the algorithm and nothing else. `StripeStrategy.execute()` only knows about Stripe. It has no branching on payment method because it *is* the payment method. This makes it:
- **Independently testable**: instantiate it directly, pass test data, assert on results.
- **Independently deployable**: in a microservices context, each strategy could even live in its own module loaded on demand.
- **Easily swappable**: adding `KlarnaStrategy` requires zero changes to existing code.

**3. Context (the orchestrator)**

The Context stores the strategy in a field (typically `_strategy` or `strategy`). It exposes:
- A way to inject a strategy: either via the constructor (`new Checkout(StripeStrategy)`) or a setter (`checkout.setStrategy(PayPalStrategy)`).
- Its own public API (`checkout.pay(amount, details)`) which delegates to `this._strategy.execute({ amount, details })`.

The Context may do work before and after delegating — logging, validation, retry logic — but the *algorithm* is never in the Context.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The before/after contrast is the core lesson. The monolithic version must be reopened for each new provider; the after version is genuinely closed for modification — adding Klarna required zero changes to Checkout. Notice that strategies are plain objects in JS, not classes — duck typing removes the need for formal inheritance.

sections.caption: Two injection points: factory-based selection at startup from config, and runtime swap via setStrategy() from user interaction. The Context handles both transparently.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Function-based strategies are idiomatic JavaScript — Array.sort() itself is exactly this pattern. The getSortStrategy factory decouples string-based user input from algorithm selection. The Sorter context never changes regardless of how many sort strategies you add.

sections.title: Strategy vs. Related Patterns: Precise Distinctions
sections.content:
The Strategy pattern is frequently confused with three closely related patterns. Understanding the distinctions sharpens your design instincts.

**Strategy vs. Template Method**

Template Method (another GoF behavioural pattern) also addresses algorithm variation, but uses **inheritance** instead of composition. A base class defines the skeleton of an algorithm and declares abstract methods for the variable steps. Subclasses fill in those steps. The algorithm structure is fixed in the superclass; subclasses override specific hooks.

Key difference: Template Method is a compile-time decision through inheritance hierarchy. You cannot switch the algorithm variant at runtime. Strategy uses composition and a field reference — you can hot-swap strategies without creating a new Context. Use Template Method when the algorithm skeleton is invariant and you only need to customise specific steps. Use Strategy when the entire algorithm, or large parts of it, vary and need runtime flexibility.

**Strategy vs. Command**

Both patterns encapsulate behaviour in an object. The intent differs:
- **Strategy**: One algorithm active at a time, selected to do a job. Strategies are generally stateless and interchangeable. The Context has a single strategy slot.
- **Command**: Encapsulates a *request* as an object — with receiver, action, and parameters bundled together. Commands can be queued, logged, serialised, executed in sequence, and **undone** (via an `undo()` method). Multiple commands can stack. The pattern is about controlling the *execution* of requests, not selecting among algorithm variants.

A payment system might use both: Strategy selects *how* to charge (Stripe vs. PayPal); Command wraps each charge as an undoable operation for a refund trail.

**Strategy vs. State**

State pattern also involves swapping an internal object at runtime. The difference is in who triggers the swap and why:
- **Strategy**: The *client* chooses and sets the strategy. The strategy itself has no agency over which strategy comes next. It is purely algorithmic.
- **State**: The state objects themselves trigger transitions to other states. The Context is passive; state objects drive the lifecycle. State is about modelling a finite state machine.

A vending machine modelled with State has states (Idle, HasCoin, Dispensing) that transition each other. A sorting widget modelled with Strategy has an external user selecting the sort algorithm — the strategy has no knowledge of other strategies.

sections.caption: Decision tree for choosing among Strategy, Template Method, State, and Command. Strategy is the choice when the client selects among interchangeable algorithms and runtime swapping is needed.

sections.title: Testing Strategies in Isolation and Testing the Context
Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases

sections.content: **Historical context:** The Strategy pattern was documented by the Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides) in *Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software* (1994). The motivating example in the book was a text layout algorithm — different line-breaking strategies for a document editor. The pattern predates the book; Smalltalk programmers had been using the concept for years. The insight was naming and formalising it so teams could communicate about the structure precisely. Today, Strategy is arguably the most practised GoF pattern in production JavaScript, even by developers who do not know it by name — every time you pass a `compareFn` to `Array.sort()`, you are the client of a Strategy-based API.

**When to use Strategy:**
- You have a growing `if/else` or `switch` that selects among algorithm variants based on a type or configuration.
- Different variants of an algorithm need to be tested in isolation.
- Algorithms need to be selected at runtime (from config, user input, or environment).
- You want to comply with the Open/Closed Principle: new variants should not require modifying the Context.

**When NOT to use Strategy:**
- Only one algorithm exists and no variants are anticipated (YAGNI).
- The 'algorithms' share no common interface at all — a factory function or simple module import may be simpler.
- The variation is trivial (one parameter difference) — just pass the parameter instead of creating a strategy object.
- The strategies need to transition into each other based on internal logic — that is the State pattern.

**Real frameworks that use Strategy:** Passport.js (auth strategies), webpack (loaders), Joi/Yup/Zod (validation schemas), `Array.sort(compareFn)`, `Intl.Collator`, Lodash `_.sortBy`, Axios interceptors, Jest's `testEnvironment` configuration, NestJS guards and interceptors.

items: **The core idea is delegation over branching:** instead of a `switch` on algorithm type inside the Context, the Context holds a `_strategy` reference and calls `execute()` — the algorithm lives entirely in the strategy object.

**Compose, don't inherit:** Strategy uses a field (composition) rather than subclassing. This enables runtime algorithm swapping — something inheritance cannot provide — and avoids the fragile base-class problem.
**Open/Closed Principle in practice:** adding a new algorithm means writing a new ConcreteStrategy class or object; the Context is never modified. This is the pattern's primary design value.
**Testability is a first-class benefit:** each strategy can be unit tested in complete isolation; the Context can be tested with a stub strategy — no real external service is needed for either test.

**In JavaScript, strategies are duck-typed:** any object with the expected method, or any function with the right signature, qualifies as a strategy — no formal interfaces or class hierarchies required.

**Distinguish from related patterns:** Template Method varies algorithms via inheritance (compile-time, not runtime); Command encapsulates requests with undo/queue semantics; State has objects that drive their own transitions. Strategy is client-controlled, runtime-swappable, and purely algorithmic.

**The pattern is everywhere:** `Array.sort(compareFn)`, Passport.js, webpack loaders, and Yup/Zod schemas are all mainstream JavaScript APIs built on the Strategy pattern — recognising it there cements the concept.

quiz.question: What structural problem does the Strategy pattern primarily solve in a class like Checkout?
options: It ensures only one Checkout instance exists at a time.
It eliminates a growing if/switch block of algorithm variants inside the Context, replacing it with delegation to interchangeable strategy objects.
It provides a simplified facade over multiple payment SDKs.
It queues payment requests so they can be retried or undone.
quiz.explanation: Strategy extracts each algorithm variant into its own object, removing branching from the Context. The Context delegates to whichever strategy is active rather than containing all variants itself.

quiz.question: Which JavaScript built-in API is the most direct everyday example of the Strategy pattern?
options: JSON.stringify(value, replacer)
Promise.race(promises)
Array.prototype.sort(compareFn)
Object.assign(target, source)
quiz.explanation: Array.sort(compareFn) accepts a comparison strategy as a parameter. The sorting engine (TimSort) is the fixed Context; the comparison function is the injected ConcreteStrategy. The array is oblivious to how comparison works.

quiz.question: How does Strategy differ from the Template Method pattern?
options: Template Method uses composition; Strategy uses inheritance.
Strategy uses composition (a field reference) enabling runtime swapping; Template Method uses inheritance to fill in algorithm steps at compile time.
Template Method is for sorting; Strategy is for payment processing.
Strategy requires a formal abstract base class; Template Method does not.
quiz.explanation: Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton in a base class with abstract steps overridden by subclasses — a static, inheritance-based approach. Strategy stores the algorithm in a field and can swap it at runtime — a dynamic, composition-based approach.

quiz.question: In Passport.js, which component plays the role of 'Context' in the Strategy pattern?
options: The Express app object.
The req.user property populated after authentication.
Passport itself, which delegates authentication to whichever strategy is registered.
The JWT token returned after login.
quiz.explanation: Passport is the Context — it holds registered strategies and delegates authentication to the appropriate one. LocalStrategy, JwtStrategy, and OAuth2Strategy are the ConcreteStrategies. Client routes call passport.authenticate() without knowing which strategy runs.

quiz.question: What does Context.setStrategy(s) enable that subclassing a Context class does not?
options: Access to private fields within the strategy.
Calling multiple strategies simultaneously for redundancy.
Swapping the algorithm at runtime without creating a new Context object.
Inheriting configuration state from the previous strategy.
quiz.explanation: setStrategy() replaces the _strategy field reference mid-lifecycle. The same Context object runs a completely different algorithm from that point onward. Subclassing is a compile-time decision — you cannot change a subclass at runtime without destroying and recreating the object.

quiz.question: Which SOLID principle does the Strategy pattern most directly embody?
options: Liskov Substitution Principle — strategies are substitutable for one another.
Open/Closed Principle — the Context is open for extension via new strategies but closed for modification.
Interface Segregation Principle — the strategy interface is kept narrow.
Dependency Inversion Principle — the Context depends on an abstraction.
quiz.explanation: Adding a new algorithm requires only adding a new ConcreteStrategy — the Context is never modified. This is the Open/Closed Principle in its clearest practical form. (Note: Dependency Inversion is also satisfied, but OCP is the primary intent.)

quiz.question: What is the key structural difference between Strategy and Command patterns?
options: Strategy objects can be undone; Command objects cannot.
Command uses composition; Strategy uses inheritance.
Strategy replaces a whole algorithm — one active at a time; Command encapsulates a request that can be queued, logged, and undone.
They are identical patterns with different names in different books.
quiz.explanation: Strategy is about selecting among interchangeable algorithms (mutually exclusive, stateless). Command is about encapsulating requests as objects that can stack, be queued, serialised, and reversed via undo(). Different intents, different structures.

quiz.question: In JavaScript, what is the minimum requirement for an object to qualify as a ConcreteStrategy?
options: It must extend a formal Strategy base class or implement a TypeScript interface.
It must be decorated with a @Injectable() annotation for DI.
It must satisfy the method signature the Context expects — duck typing means no formal inheritance is required.
It must be a singleton registered in a global registry.
quiz.explanation: JavaScript uses duck typing. Any object or function that has the expected method (e.g., execute(data)) qualifies as a strategy. Plain objects, closures, class instances, and arrow functions all work — no formal inheritance or annotation is required.

quiz.question: When is Strategy NOT a good fit — and a simpler approach should be preferred?
options: When multiple algorithm variants exist and need to be tested in isolation.
When the algorithm must be selected from a config file at startup.
When there is only one algorithm and no credible second variant is anticipated.
When different teams own different algorithm implementations.
quiz.explanation: YAGNI — if there is only one algorithm today and no anticipated variants, extracting it into a strategy object adds pointless indirection. Introduce Strategy when the second variant appears, or when test isolation alone justifies the abstraction.

quiz.question: A Checkout receives its payment strategy via constructor injection. Which testing benefit does this directly provide?
options: The Checkout class can extend multiple strategy classes at once.
Tests can inject a stub strategy object — { execute: jest.fn() } — without hitting real payment APIs, isolating the Context's logic.
The strategy is automatically selected based on the NODE_ENV variable.
The Checkout class becomes thread-safe across concurrent requests.
quiz.explanation: Constructor injection makes the dependency explicit and replaceable. A test passes a stub strategy object (e.g., { execute: jest.fn().mockReturnValue({ success: true }) }) — no Stripe or PayPal network calls occur. This isolates and tests the Context's orchestration logic (error handling, logging, validation) independently of any real payment provider.
